Management Plan
2026
Eurostat
1

PART 1. Introduction
Eurostat is the statistical authority of the European Union. Eurostat provides reliable and
comparable statistical information to support evidence-based policymaking in the EU and the
implementation of the Commission’s political priorities. To this end, Eurostat develops and
promotes standards, methods, procedures, practices and tools that enable the cost-effective
development, production and dissemination of high-quality European statistics.
European statistics are developed, produced and disseminated in line with the principles
enshrined in Article 338 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union and further
elaborated in Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 (1) on European statistics and the European
Statistics Code of Practice. Eurostat’s activities are governed by professional independence,
impartial treatment of all users, objectivity, reliability, statistical confidentiality and cost-
effectiveness. Under Commission Decision 2012/504/EU (2), Eurostat also coordinates the
development and production of statistics produced by other Commission services.
Eurostat is assisted by two advisory bodies: the European Statistical Governance Advisory
Board, which focuses on the European Statistics Code of Practice; and the European Statistical
Advisory Committee, which gives its opinion on the European multiannual and annual statistical
programmes, focusing on matters of relevance to users and adequacy of resources.
Eurostat carries out its mission in partnership with the EU Member States. National statistical
institutes (NSIs) and other national authorities designated to produce official statistics make up
the European Statistical System (ESS). EEA EFTA States (Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway) and
Switzerland also participate in the ESS under specific agreements. In addition, Eurostat
cooperates closely with the European Central Bank and other international organisations to lead
the development of international standards and so ensure the comparability of statistics
throughout the world.
Strategic planning and programming is the cornerstone of the Commission’s performance
management framework. The Commission’s strategic plan for 2025-2029 translates the
political priorities set in the Political Guidelines of President von der Leyen into general
objectives. This process ensures institutional coherence, enhances accountability, and aligns the
actions of all Commission services with the strategic vision of the mandate. Within this
framework, each Commission service has developed a strategic outlook for 2025-2029 in

3

their 2025 management plan. This outlook defines a set of multiannual objectives and
indicators to measure progress towards their achievement. These will be used for planning and
reporting on performance throughout the period.
Eurostat’s 2026 management plan sets out how Eurostat will contribute to these
multiannual objectives (Part 2) and to the common objective of building a modern and
sustainable public administration (Part 3). The main outputs with their indicators and targets
are presented in Annexes 1 and 2.
The figure below illustrates the performance framework for Eurostat.
Figure 1 – Overview of the Commission’s general objectives, Eurostat’s specific objectives and
the key performance indicators
The chart shows the Commission’s eight general objectives, Eurostat’s specific objectives
contributing to each general objective and the key performance indicators measuring the
contribution. Eurostat has defined three specific objectives and three key performance indicators.
Specific Objective 1: Eurostat provides enriched and more attractive statistics and data in support of
the Commission’s priorities and effective policy implementation. Specific Objective 1 contributes to
General Objectives 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 7. It is measured by the key performance indicator ‘European
Commission users’ satisfaction with data and services’.
Specific Objective 2: Eurostat supports national statistical systems in enlargement countries and
strengthens international statistical partnerships. Specific Objective 2 contributes to General
4

Objective 6. It is measured by the key performance indicator ‘increased availability of validated
statistical data produced by enlargement countries in Eurostat’s public dissemination database’.
Specific Objective 3: Eurostat strengthens its role as the trusted reference point for statistics and
data on Europe using digital technologies, new data sources, revamped legal frameworks and
improved communication. Specific Objective 3 contributes to General Objectives 5 and 8. It is
measured by the key performance indicator ‘trust in European statistics’.
Source: Eurostat
5

PART 2. Delivering on the Commission’s
priorities in 2026
General Objective 1: a new plan for Europe’s
sustainable prosperity and competitiveness
Specific Objective 1.1: Eurostat provides enriched and more attractive statistics and data in
support of the Commission’s priorities and effective policy implementation.
A key initiative for Eurostat in 2026 will be the preparation of draft Commission proposals for a
new regulation on the European system of national and regional accounts in the European
Union and a new regulation on European statistics concerning balance of payments,
international trade in services and foreign direct investment (FDI). These proposals will reflect
two recently adopted international statistical standards (the 2025 System of National Accounts
and Balance of Payment Manual (seventh edition) respectively). The updates aim at better
integrating digitalisation, sustainability and well-being into the framework for measuring
the economic activities of EU Member States and ensuring its international
comparability.
Eurostat will enhance the timeliness of the set of macroeconomic globalisation
indicators in order to provide better insights into the EU’s global interactions, leading to more
accurate and agile policies for strengthening the EU’s economic resilience and competitiveness.
Eurostat will also improve and expand the available labour and capital productivity indicators,
further develop the experimental statistics on multifactor productivity, and improve their
accessibility by publishing a dedicated EU productivity dashboard.
In February 2026 (with the release of the flash Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) for
January 2026), several methodological and practical improvements will be implemented to
make the HICP more relevant and more accurately represent developments in the prices of
all goods and services available to consumers. Firstly, the updated United Nations
Classification of Individual Consumption According to Purpose 2018 will be introduced.
Secondly, games of chance as a recreation service – for which a new methodology has been
developed – will be included in the HICP’s scope for the first time. Thirdly, the indices will be
rebased to a new common index reference year (2025 instead of 2015). All these changes are
the results of a joint project with Member States that since 2018 ensures coordination,
legislative updates, methodological harmonisation and comparability of statistics.
Eurostat will continue to provide high-quality statistics for the excessive deficit procedure,
supporting the EU economic governance framework and EU fiscal oversight. Business and
trade statistics will continue to feed into the monitoring of implementation of the European
industrial strategy. Trade in goods statistics will continue to provide timely and detailed data
for monitoring the impact of the EU’s free trade agreements with non-EU countries. To
support international trade negotiations, Eurostat will from 2026 annually disseminate
6

statistics on international trade in services, by mode of supply and trade in services by
enterprise characteristics. Eurostat will continue to work in collaboration with the national
statistical authorities to reduce bilateral statistical asymmetries in international trade
in services between the EU Member States and with key trade partners. The use of microdata
that have been exchanged for the compilation of trade statistics will continue to contribute to
the reduction of the reporting burden, especially on SMEs.
Eurostat will continue to contribute to the Commission’s simplification priorities. As indicated
in the multiannual stress testing plan 2025-2029 and the Commission Work Programme 2026,
in Q3 2026, Eurostat is performing a wide-ranging evaluation which relates to as many as 20
statistical products – the evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2019/2152 on European business
statistics aiming to further identify areas for simplification and burden reduction by identifying
alternative data sources and new production methods. Both the evaluation of the Regulation on
European business statistics and the upcoming Commission proposal to amend Regulation (EU)
2018/1091 on integrated farm statistics (see general objective 4) will contribute to the
Commission-wide target of reducing administrative burdens by 25% for businesses (35% for
SMEs). Eurostat will continue organising reality checks, focusing in 2026 on waste statistics,
energy statistics, and social statistics. Finally, Eurostat will continue to support the organisation
of Commissioner Dombrovskis’ implementation dialogues and to contribute to the
Commissioner’s Annual Progress Report on Simplification, Implementation and
Enforcement.
Innovative projects to link microdata from different sources will make progress with the aim of
providing new insights into EU businesses’ dependencies on imports of critical raw
materials, net-zero industry technologies and other sensitive goods from non-EU
countries. It is expected that the first results will be published in the third quarter of 2026. The
EuroGroups register will, alongside the European profiling programme, continue to
provide the core infrastructure on multinational enterprise groups operating in the EU to
make it possible to provide statistical insights into the way these enterprises restructure and
reorganise their business models in line with the changing international landscape. Work on
methods for producing early estimates of short-term business indicators using
alternative data sources or models and on nowcasting indicators from structural business
statistics will also continue in 2026. To monitor the diffusion of digital technologies, Eurostat
will continue to collect data on the digitalisation of EU companies, focusing on the adoption
of technologies such as cloud technology, AI and cybersecurity.
Eurostat will continue to improve collection of data on FDI inward positions (by the
ultimate investing economy), while also paving the way for new statistics such as FDI (by
the ultimate host economy). Eurostat will continue to work on reducing bilateral statistical
asymmetries between Member States in FDI and foreign affiliates statistics (FATS), in the
contexts of the FDI network and the FATS asymmetries resolution mechanism respectively.
To support the monitoring of the green transition with reliable data, the community
innovation survey will include information on the perceived impact of climate change on
businesses in the EU. In 2026, the Member States will report for the first time on
environmental subsidies under Regulation (EU) No 691/2011 on European environmental
economic accounts. These data are necessary in order to underpin the EU’s environmental and
7

climate policies. Transport decarbonisation will be supported with improved indicators on the
shift of goods and passengers from more-polluting to less-polluting modes of transport
(including the contribution of oil pipelines to the total transport of goods). Eurostat will perform
a reality check on energy statistics, focusing on Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 on energy
statistics, in the first half of 2026.
Eurostat will publish data on electricity and gas prices paid by households and industrial
consumers to help monitor energy affordability and the competitiveness of EU
industries. In collaboration with DG ENER and DG CLIMA, Eurostat will continue developing an
IT tool that prevents double-reporting under the Energy Union Governance and the Renewable
Energy Directive. A priority for Eurostat in 2026 will be the preparation of an amendment of
Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 on energy statistics in response to changing information needs
related to the Clean Industrial Deal.
With the aim of filling significant gaps in the field of non-financial commercial real estate
statistics needed for macro-prudential purposes at both EU and national level, the
Commission adopted a Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the
Council (3) on 11 March 2025. Once adopted, the statistics will be used to monitor financial
stability and for fiscal, monetary and macro-prudential policymaking and for research on real
estate markets.
In line with the aim of putting research and innovation at the heart of the economy and their
role in Europe’s competitiveness, Eurostat will continue to produce statistics on research and
development investments by EU companies and the public sector.
General Objective 2: a new era for European
defence and security
Specific Objective 2.1: Eurostat provides enriched and more attractive statistics and data in
support of the Commission’s priorities and effective policy implementation.
Eurostat’s work in support of General Objective 2 will respond to the policy needs set out in the
White Paper for the Future of European Defence and the Commission Communication on
‘Accommodating increased defence expenditure within the Stability and Growth Pact’. Eurostat
will play a key role in providing timely data for the consistent application of the national escape
clause through improved data collection based on the European system of national and
regional accounts and aligned with the transmission deadlines for the excessive deficit
procedure. Eurostat will also continue preparing methodological guidance on statistical
recording of investments in defence. As part of the microdata linking programme, Eurostat will,
together with the Member States, start compiling business and trade statistics for enterprises
(3) Proposal for a Regulation of the European Parliament and of the Council on non-financial commercial
real estate statistics, COM/2025/100 final, 2025/0052(COD), 11.3.2025.
8

active in the defence and space sectors without creating additional reporting burden for EU
businesses.
In line with the Vision for the European Space Economy, Eurostat will further develop and
publish statistics on the European space economy, focusing on estimating the extent to which
different industries and products are relevant to the space economy.
Eurostat will, together with the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA), prepare a new data
flow model for international protection statistics. The aim will be to improve the timeliness
and relevance of European official statistics on international protection and their use
in the European annual asylum and migration report, as well as to eliminate existing
discrepancies in data published by different public bodies and reduce the reporting burden
on national administrations.
General Objective 3: supporting people, and
strengthening our societies and our social
models
Specific Objective 3.1: Eurostat provides enriched and more attractive statistics and data in
support of the Commission’s priorities and effective policy implementation.
Eurostat has developed a wide range of transversal indicators and datasets to inform and
evaluate policy decisions. These include the social scoreboard of the European Pillar of
Social Rights, a quality of life indicator set, statistics on youth and children, equality
and non-discrimination statistics, sport statistics and culture statistics. In 2026,
Eurostat will continue providing key monthly labour market indicators (i.e. on
unemployment) and quarterly indicators on job vacancies, labour costs and labour market slack.
Data on the reconciliation of work and family life in 2025 and the first results from the
2024 labour cost survey will also be released in 2026. A dedicated labour force survey module
on digital platform employment will be carried out. Following the entry into force of the
revised regulation on EU labour market statistics on businesses in June 2025, Eurostat will
prepare the implementing acts for the 4-yearly labour cost survey and for quality reporting.
Eurostat will continue releasing specific indicators from the latest wave of the time-use survey.
These provide valuable information on how people allocate their time, thereby allowing a better
understanding of the relationship between work, care and leisure activities.
In 2026, Eurostat will provide new data on aspects of energy and the environment,
categorised by poverty status and various socio-economic factors. Eurostat will continue
producing model-based early estimates of income distribution and poverty indicators for
the needs of the European Semester. To further improve the understanding of people’s
economic well-being, Eurostat will publish the latest experimental data on household
distributional accounts for income and consumption.
9

Population statistics and demography data remain highly relevant for the Commission’s
policy agenda in the context of an ageing society, a shrinking working age population and the
availability of skills. In 2026, Eurostat will focus its efforts on developing implementing
measures for the new Regulation (EU) 2025/2458 on European statistics on population
and housing that will apply from 1 January 2028. This includes the preparations for annually
producing data that are georeferenced to a harmonised EU-wide 1 km2 grid, the new
multiannual data collection and the 2031 EU population and housing census round.
Eurostat will publish the next long-term population projections that will be used as input for
various policies (such as the EU’s cohesion policies) for assessing the long-term sustainability
of public finances or analysing the impact of ageing populations on the European labour market
and economic growth.
Healthcare expenditure and non-expenditure statistics, as well as statistics on causes of
death, will support healthcare policies and the European care strategy. Long-term care
statistics will be developed. Eurostat will publish a report on the project of creating
occupational diseases statistics to support the European Pillar of Social Rights.
Eurostat will also expand the experimental statistics on skill demands, using web-scraped
data from online job advertisements as a basis.
Eurostat will further develop equality and non-discrimination statistics, and improve their
availability. Furthermore, a dedicated task force of NSIs, EU agencies and main users will
continue working on guidelines for better harmonisation, coverage and inclusiveness of these
statistics.
Eurostat’s internal task force on housing statistics will continue to support the
Commission’s European affordable housing plan. Eurostat will map the available and
upcoming statistics and publications on housing produced by Eurostat, including through a
dedicated landing page on Eurostat’s website. Eurostat will launch outreach and communication
activities to promote its housing-related data and statistics among the relevant stakeholders. It
will also monitor emerging data needs. In the context of the Commission’s objective of creating
a pan-European investment platform for affordable and sustainable housing, Eurostat will
clarify the investment scenarios by analysing how fiscal rules apply to the main practices within
the sector, thereby helping to assess the impact on government finance.
The information and communication technologies statistics will produce high-quality data
on the digitalisation of EU society. This will be used to monitor the progress of the Digital
Decade policy, with a special focus on the digital skills of EU citizens and their use of artificial
intelligence.
Eurostat will perform a reality check on social statistics, focusing on the implementation of
Regulation (EU) 2019/1700 establishing a common framework for European statistics relating
to persons and households, based on data at individual level collected from samples, and the
supporting regulations for the labour force domain and income and living conditions domain.
10

General Objective 4: sustaining our quality of
life: food security, water and nature
Specific Objective 4.1: Eurostat provides enriched and more attractive statistics and data in
support of the Commission’s priorities and effective policy implementation.
One priority for Eurostat in 2026 will be the preparation of a draft Commission proposal to
amend Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 on integrated farm statistics. This would introduce the
legal basis for farm data collection for 2030-2039 as well as enhance efficiency and reduce
the reporting burden on farmers through increased reuse of administrative and new digital data
sources, more specifically by: i) promoting more modern data collection techniques, e.g. digital
tools; ii) allowing more flexibility in data collection processes; iii) defining an appropriate census
and/or survey coverage, periodicity, and sample size; and iv) broadening the possibility to use
suitable national data sources. The proposal will take into account the outcomes from
Commissioner Dombrovskis’s implementation dialogue on agricultural statistics and from a
series of public consultations and discussions with users and producers of these statistics.
Furthermore, Eurostat conducted in 2025 a thorough reality check which revealed general
satisfaction with Regulation (EU) 2018/1091 for its significant role in the agricultural statistics.
However, the review also pinpointed areas for enhancement, particularly concerning the burden
associated with the number of variables and the complexity of certain modules.
Following the first year implementing Regulation (EU) 2022/2379 on statistics on
agricultural input and output, comprehensive annual data on crops and animal production
(including regional and organic statistics) and agricultural price statistics will be published in
2026. 2026 is also the reference year for statistics on nutrients and grassland management.
Eurostat will put forward a proposal for an implementing act on plant protection products for
the reference years from 2028 onwards.
Throughout 2026, Eurostat will assist the co-legislators in negotiations on the Commission’s
2025 Proposal for a Regulation on fisheries and aquaculture statistics (4), mentioned in
Annex 3 of the Commission Work Programme 2026.
2026 will be the first year of mandatory reporting by Member States of ecosystem accounts
under Regulation (EU) No 691/2011 on European environmental economic accounts. Data will
be collected on ecosystem extent, condition (i.e. ‘degradation’) and ecosystem services such as
pollination and carbon absorption by forests or peatlands. These data are necessary for natural
capital, biodiversity, climate, water and forestry-related thematic policies.
In 2026 Eurostat will work with other Commission services to make the next round of the EU-
wide land use and land cover survey (LUCAS) simpler and more cost-efficient. LUCAS collects
on-site information on land cover, use, soils, ecosystems and other agri-environmental
parameters and cross-validates the results of Copernicus products and services. Eurostat will
develop new geographical accessibility indicators for services based on the existing grid
(4) Proposal for a Regulation on fisheries and aquaculture statistics (COM(2025)435 final 2025/0246 (COD)
30.07.2025.
11

population data (e.g. electrical charging stations) and explore the potential of Earth Observation
for Statistics on energy (solar panel detection) or environment (air pollution indicators).
General Objective 5: protecting our democracy,
upholding our values
Specific Objective 5.1: Eurostat provides enriched and more attractive statistics and data in
support of the Commission’s priorities and effective policy implementation.
Specific Objective 5.2: Eurostat strengthens its role as the trusted reference point for statistics
and data on Europe using digital technologies, new data sources, revamped legal frameworks
and improved communication.
Trustworthy and high-quality official statistics and data play a central role in the democratic
process. As AI increasingly shapes how people find and use data, Eurostat will continue to
strengthen its role as the reference point for trusted European statistics and contribute to
Commission initiatives to combat disinformation. Eurostat will continue to strengthen public
trust in its statistics and data and to counter disinformation with verified, authoritative data by
promoting transparency, safeguarding data privacy, clearly and actively communicating
with users and collaborating with its partners across the ESS and with other institutions.
People’s trust in European statistics will be enhanced by launching more customised tools
and communication outputs, branding promotional activities tailored to various stakeholders,
improving statistical literacy, expanding Eurostat’s social media presence and providing media
and factcheckers with accurate information in a timely manner.
The monitoring of the implementation of the improvement actions from the third round of peer
reviews in the ESS will continue in 2026.
General Objective 6: a global Europe: leveraging
our power and partnerships
Specific Objective 6.1: Eurostat supports national statistical systems in enlargement countries
and strengthens international statistical partnerships.
Eurostat will continue its active cooperation with international organisations (e.g. UN, OECD,
IMF, ILO and World Bank) to set international statistical standards and promote EU
values and the principles of the European Statistics Code of Practice. Eurostat will also
collaborate with European Neighbourhood Policy countries to obtain comparable energy
statistics, highlighting the role that this region is playing in the EU energy transition (e.g. with
respect to hydrogen or solar energy).
Eurostat will continue to support enlargement and neighbourhood countries, using EU
instruments to increase the availability of high-quality official statistics. Cooperation with the
enlargement countries will focus on increasing the availability of acquis compliant statistics.
12

Furthermore, Eurostat will develop a new strategy for statistical cooperation for the period of
the next multi-annual financial framework. Statistical cooperation with Mediterranean countries
will follow the Pact for the Mediterranean and its action plan, including the development of a
statistical cooperation strategy with Southern Mediterranean countries for 2028–2034 to
strengthen collaboration with their National Statistical Institutes. Support to statistical
institutions in Africa will continue in line with EU priorities.
General Objective 7: delivering together and
preparing our Union for the future
Specific Objective 7.1: Eurostat provides enriched and more attractive statistics and data in
support of the Commission’s priorities and effective policy implementation.
In June 2026, Eurostat will release the new editions of the report on the EU’s progress towards
the 17 Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and of the Regional Yearbook report.
Eurostat will continue to publish the monthly European Statistical Monitor (ESM) dashboard and
related commentary, which together provide a holistic overview and show key economic,
environmental and labour market developments and trends across the EU and the
European Free Trade Association (EFTA).
As part of its offer of statistical data based on geospatial information, Eurostat will
update the Statistical Atlas with the latest information from the population census, farming and
land cover surveys. Eurostat will continue providing the Commission services with infrastructure
for geospatial services such as map-making.
In 2026, Eurostat will complete the first verification cycle of Member States regarding the
plastic-based own resource. Eurostat will also support the Council’s discussions on a
possible, future own resource on e-waste. In autumn 2026, Eurostat will organise a reality
check on waste statistics.
In relation to gross national income-based own resource purposes, Eurostat will perform a risk
analysis as the basis for the information visits programme and structuring verification in the
current 2025-2029 cycle.
In 2026, Eurostat will carry out the family budget survey to update consumption weights for
calculating the joint Brussels-Luxembourg index, which is used for the calculation of EU and
international staff remuneration, and the intra-EU Staff Housing Survey.
General Objective 8: a modern, high-performing
and sustainable European Commission
Specific Objective 8.1: Eurostat strengthens its role as the trusted reference point for statistics
and data on Europe using digital technologies, new data sources, revamped legal frameworks
and improved communication.
13

2026 will be the second year of implementing the amended Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 on
European statistics that will enable Eurostat, as part of a modern and high-performing
Commission, and the ESS as a whole to produce high-quality, trustworthy European statistics
more innovatively and efficiently as well as to fully exploit digital data sources and
technologies, securing sustainable access to new data sources and better addressing
evolving user needs. Eurostat will, in close cooperation with the Member States, draw up
guidelines for engaging with private data-holders, and prepare strategies and roadmaps for the
use of privately-held data in four statistical priority domains. It will also implement the
reference framework for the development phase of European statistics. In this regard, Eurostat
will make further progress in implementing the ESS Innovation Agenda, a strategic framework
that coordinates innovation efforts across the ESS.
Eurostat will continue disseminating European statistics and data free of charge, in an
impartial, accessible and understandable manner. By adapting to technological advances
and the needs of different user-groups, Eurostat will disseminate products and services that
are inclusive, coherent and visible across various communication channels, in line with
Eurostat’s communication and dissemination strategy for 2025-2029 and its annual
dissemination and communication programmes.
Eurostat will further implement its digital-by-default approach to the dissemination of
statistics and data by promoting interactive digital publications, visualisation tools, dashboards,
webinars and podcasts that make statistics easier to understand and reuse. This includes
Eurostat products that are easily discoverable by both people and AI-based search engines,
with simplified content and adapted communication styles for different social media platforms.
In 2026, Eurostat will further improve services related to accessing European microdata for
researchers by making available additional datasets to support academic research in new
areas, such as demand for skills.
Eurostat will also continue to provide high-quality training in cutting-edge statistical
fields (such as AI, Earth Observation and the use of internet sources for compiling official
statistics) via the European Statistical Training Programme (ESTP) to statisticians across
Europe. Eurostat will lead the implementation of the European Master in Official Statistics
(EMOS) programme in line with its revamped mission, goals, values and learning outcomes. In
addition, the EMOS network will continue rolling out and promoting its new mobility
programme, fostering collaboration in European statistical education and intensifying
communication between member organisations with the aim of supporting the ESS in recruiting
and retaining staff with sufficient skills to meet future challenges.
As set out in the Mission Letter for Commissioner Dombrovskis and on a Simpler and Faster
Europe, Eurostat is organising Commissioner Dombrovskis' implementation dialogues on
European official statistics and will contribute to the Commissioner’s progress report on the
enforcement and implementation of the statistical acquis.
For details of the outputs, please refer to the performance tables in Annex 1 (pp. 21-27).
14

PART 3. A modern and sustainable public
administration: outputs in 2026
A. Human resource management
In 2026, Eurostat will continue to focus on ensuring effective management of human resources
to deliver on the Commission’s and Eurostat’s priorities. To prepare for the challenges of
technological advancements and the ever-increasing needs for statistical data, Eurostat will
continue to place a particular focus on staff training, learning and development.
Eurostat will continue to implement the new recruitment model developed by DG HR,
following the two open EPSO AD competitions specialised in the fields of ‘statistics’ and
‘economics’, and the competition in the fields of data management and data knowledge for
Luxembourg. This will help Eurostat to respond to the high number of expected retirements in
the next few years (nearly 20% of statutory staff during 2025-2029). Newcomers will benefit
from the improved onboarding scheme in Eurostat that includes (a) a mentor for each
newcomer to facilitate their integration into the workplace; and (b) a roadmap for the recruiting
unit to ensure successful onboarding. Eurostat will also contribute to all measures that aim at
making Luxembourg more attractive as a workplace.
Eurostat will seek to maintain the gender balance among middle managers (female
representation was 56.6% at the end of 2025) and will continue to make gender-balanced first
appointments at the middle-management level. Eurostat will use all its allocated quota for the
corporate management development programme. Eurostat will further support the
Commission’s policy on geographical balance by publishing all vacancies for external
staff on EPSO’s and Eurostat’s websites. This will help Eurostat to identify more candidates,
including ones from under-represented nationalities. Directors will also continue to ensure that
their directorates have a geographically-balanced approach to recruitment.
Eurostat will develop and implement the follow-up activities from the results of the 2025
Commission staff survey and will aim to maintain high staff engagement. Regular meetings
between staff and senior management on HR-related and work-related matters will continue.
The Director-General will continue to meet newcomers during their induction sessions.
Eurostat will continue to invest in its internal communication to inform staff about ongoing
developments on business and HR-related topics, to facilitate knowledge-transfer and
communication between senior management and staff, and to promote the Commission’s new
digital tools to support Eurostat staff.
15

B. Digital transformation and data management
Digital transformation and digital culture
Eurostat is an active member of the Commission’s digital transformation community. It
contributes to implement the Commission’s digital strategy and participates in several
corporate initiatives and groups to advance the digital transformation in the Commission – to
mention a few: the Digital Stakeholders Forum, the Cloud Council, the DevSecOps Community
of Practice, the Data Analytics and Business Intelligence (DABI) Users Group and the Digital
WorkPlace User Group. With the same intent, Eurostat also runs a number of internal groups
such as the Eurostat IT Forum and the Community of Practice for the modernisation of the
Statistical Production Systems.
Eurostat will continue to promote the digital culture and will further facilitate the adoption of
modern digital collaboration working methods by participating in IT trainings, particularly on
topics closest to Eurostat’s needs (i.e. statistical data processing, digital collaboration and AI).
Eurostat will continue to modernise its IT landscape and systems in line with the Commission’s
digital strategy. Cloud adoption is considered an essential enabler for statistical production, so
Eurostat will continue transitioning the current IT systems to the cloud-based solution where
applicable. Eurostat is committed to promote a secure deployment of new Cloud workloads
using the new EC Cloud Security Controls Baseline (CSCB), the principles and rules on
outsourcing of CIS, the EC Managed Landing Zone and the recommendations of the Cloud
Council (such as the management of SNC data in IaaS and PaaS, the secure use of SaaS).
Eurostat will strive to continuously improve the security posture of existing cloud deployments,
via dedicated/specialised cloud security monitoring, incident management, lessons learnt and
managed implementation of improvement actions.
Eurostat will step up its efforts to embed AI at all stages of developing, producing and
disseminating EU statistics. It will also use AI in routine activities to enhance internal
efficiency.
Eurostat will continue to adhere to the Commission’s digital-ready policymaking framework
(digital checks, digital-ready guidance, and digital statements) and consider the need for an
interoperability assessment for its policy proposals.
Cybersecurity and business continuity
In 2026, Eurostat will continue to enhance IT security and resilience in line with the
Commission’s strategies (including a comprehensive review of all the Information Systems’ IT
security plans to ensure that they are up to date). Eurostat will implement the actions laid down
in the Commission’s Cybersecurity Strategy for 2025-2026 as designated in the Commission’s
Cybersecurity Plan 2025-2026, with primary responsibilities assigned to the Directorates-
General (DGs) and Local Information Security Officers (LISOs).
Internal awareness campaigns will, in cooperation with DG DIGIT and DG HR’s security
directorate, help improve knowledge about cybersecurity through targeted training courses,
mandatory information sessions for newcomers and regular phishing exercises. Eurostat will
16

also strengthen its business continuity and disaster recovery strategies to meet new threat
scenarios and business needs.
Data management
Data management is Eurostat’s core business and it already has a well-developed data
management framework. All Eurostat’s key data assets are declared either on
data.europa.eu (the official portal for European public data assets) or in the Commission’s data
catalogue. Eurostat has established comprehensive quality frameworks for the development,
production and dissemination of statistics, also involving the Member States (for European
statistics) and other Commission departments (for ‘other’ statistics). In 2026, Eurostat intends
to identify (from the data assets it declares in the Commission’s data catalogue) a subset of
assets whose maturity will be assessed under a dedicated framework to assess data quality
and compliance with the FAIR principles. This framework is being developed by DIGIT as part of
the 2025-2029 IMSB rolling action plan. By the end of 2026, to enhance discoverability,
Eurostat will aim to better expose basic information about discontinued data assets through
the search engine on the Eurostat website by reusing metadata already available in Eurostat's
systems.
Eurostat has well-established practices for data owners and data stewards for all data
collections for statistical purposes. Eurostat will continue establishing a link between the
responsibilities of data owners and stewards with their job descriptions for its key data assets.
Eurostat will also ensure that all the data assets declared in the Commission’s data catalogue
have registered data owners and data stewards.
Eurostat’s advanced data-related expertise has allowed it to contribute to the development of
learning packages on statistics for the EU institutions’ staff. Eurostat will build on these existing
competencies and continue developing its data-related skills by taking part in corporate data
training programmes and capacity-building initiatives. Eurostat’s maturity level in implementing
corporate data policies across the four key areas (data management, ownership and
responsibilities, data quality and data skills) is assessed as established. Eurostat will strive to
reach the advanced maturity level by 2029.
Data protection
Eurostat will continue to monitor and regularly update the records of its data processing
operations in the Data Protection Management System and its training and communication
activities, ensuring that all staff members remain aware of data protection rules. In addition to
the existing training courses organised by the Commission’s data protection office, tailor-made
training for Eurostat directorates and awareness-raising activities for all newcomers have been
integrated into the newcomers’ induction programme and will continue to be delivered by
Eurostat’s data protection coordinator team. Articles will continue to be published regularly on
the intranet to promote training materials for all staff.
17

C. Sound financial management
Eurostat’s operational budget supports the implementation of the programme for the single
market, competitiveness of enterprises (including SMEs) and European statistics 2021-2027 (5),
in line with the multiannual financial framework and the Financial Regulation. Eurostat ensures
sound financial management through efficient budget planning and monitoring, effective
control of transactions, support to users and accurate reporting. As a result of these continued
efforts, the estimated ‘risk at payment’ for cost-based expenditure has remained well below
the 2% target in recent years and is expected to remain at this low level in 2026.
Eurostat will continue efforts to simplify financial procedures and adapt control systems to
evolving requirements. One priority for 2026 is the progressive onboarding of all existing and
new framework contracts in E-procurement which will necessitate modifications to various
workflows and protocols to maintain ongoing financial compliance and efficiency. In addition,
Eurostat will pilot the corporate budgetary planning solution MAPP.
The internal control framework supports sound management and decision-making. In particular,
it ensures that risks to the achievement of objectives are addressed and reduced to acceptable
levels through cost-effective controls. Eurostat has established an internal control system
tailored to its particular characteristics and circumstances. The effective functioning of this
internal control system will be assessed on an ongoing basis throughout the year and will be
subject to an annual assessment covering all internal control principles.
D. Fraud risk management
2026 will be the second year of the implementation of Eurostat’s anti-fraud strategy for 2025-
2027and the actions set out in the corresponding action plan. Eurostat will continue to give
regular presentations on anti-fraud topics during the newcomers’ induction programme, publish
awareness-raising articles on the intranet and participate in the Commission’s Fraud Prevention
and Detection Network (FPDNet).
The anti-fraud monitoring exercise is integrated into Eurostat’s semi-annual reporting to senior
management. Regular reporting is ensured as part of the annual activity report and through
internal control reports.

(EU) No 652/2014.
18

E. Sound environmental management
In line with the Commission’s communication and action plan on greening the Commission to
reach climate neutrality by 2030, Eurostat will continue to work towards the greening of its
own activities and raising environmental awareness (including through the support of Eurostat’s
internal Eco-Management and Audit Scheme (EMAS) network).
Eurostat was the first Commission DG to establish a carbon accounting system for its own
activities (this is updated annually). It will continue to monitor its carbon emissions and take
measures to lower its carbon footprint (e.g. using buildings and working space more efficiently
and sustainably, optimising its IT operations and assets, and sustainable catering).
